ctx.p1:
Cities are warmer than the countryside around them, largely because asphalt and concrete absorb heat by day and release it at night. Planting trees is the remedy most often proposed, and measurements confirm that shaded streets can be several degrees cooler than exposed ones. Yet the benefit is uneven. A tree cools mainly through evaporation from its leaves, which requires water; in dry cities, unirrigated trees close their pores during heat waves and cool the air far less at exactly the time cooling is most needed. Species matter too: a broad canopy shades more ground than a narrow one of the same height. Finally, trees take decades to mature, while reflective roofs and pavements lower surface temperatures within a season.

None of this argues against planting. It suggests that planners who count trees planted, as many programmes do, are measuring effort rather than cooling, and that the choice and care of trees deserve at least as much attention as their number.
ctx.p2:
Manufacturers have long faced a choice between variety and cost. Each additional product variant pleases some customers but adds parts to stock, tools to change and documents to maintain, and these costs are easy to overlook because they accumulate in overhead rather than in any one product's bill. Modular design is often presented as an escape from the dilemma: a limited set of standard modules is combined in different ways to yield many end products. The approach has succeeded in industries from trucks to kitchen appliances.

It is not free, however. A module designed to serve several products must meet the most demanding requirement among them, so that some products carry more capability, and more cost, than they need. Modules also fix interfaces, and an interface that is convenient today can block a better design tomorrow. Firms that benefit most tend to be those that decide deliberately where variety is visible to the customer and standardise ruthlessly everywhere else.
ctx.p3:
When a public health service set a target that patients in emergency departments be dealt with within four hours, the share of patients meeting the target rose quickly. Later analysis showed a striking pattern: a large number of patients were admitted or discharged in the final minutes before the limit. Some hospitals had also begun to hold patients in ambulances outside, since the clock started only on entry. Critics cited these findings as proof that targets corrupt the organisations they are meant to improve.

A closer study reached a more qualified conclusion. Deaths within thirty days of an emergency visit had fallen at hospitals under the target, apparently because patients with serious conditions were being admitted sooner than before. The target had produced both gaming and real improvement. The study's authors argued that the appropriate question about any measure is not whether it distorts behaviour, since all measures do, but whether the behaviour it rewards is, on balance, closer to the purpose than what went before.

ctx.s1: A foundry needs 100 kg of an alloy containing 30% nickel. It will make it by melting together alloy P, which is 20% nickel, and alloy Q, which is 60% nickel.
ctx.s2: Two contractors worked a combined 40 hours on a job. Contractor A is paid ₹500 an hour and contractor B ₹300 an hour. Together they were paid ₹17,000.
ctx.s3: A product has fixed costs of ₹30,000 a month and a variable cost of ₹150 a unit. Last month 200 units were sold and the profit was ₹10,000.

q.stem: A salary rises by 10% and then by a further 20%. The total increase is:
30% of a number is 45. What is 80% of the number?
q.why: The number is 150, and 80% of 150 is 120.

q.stem: After a 15% discount an item costs ₹1,700. Its original price was:
If x is 20% more than y, then y is what percentage less than x?
q.why: x = 1.2y, so y = x ÷ 1.2 = 0.833x, which is 16.7% less.

q.stem: Firm A's revenue rises from 250 to 300. Firm B's rises from 400 to 460. By how many percentage points does A's growth rate exceed B's?
q.why: A grew 20% and B grew 15%.

q.stem: Cement and sand are mixed in the ratio 2:5. How much cement is in 21 kg of the mix?
o: 4.2 kg
6 kg
8.4 kg
15 kg
q.why: Seven parts make 21 kg, so one part is 3 kg and cement is 6 kg.

q.stem: If a:b = 3:4 and b:c = 2:5, then a:c is:
q.why: Make b equal 4 in both: a:b = 3:4 and b:c = 4:10, so a:c = 3:10.

q.stem: ₹720 is divided among three people in the ratio 2:3:4. The largest share is:
q.why: Nine parts, each ₹80. Four parts is ₹320.

q.stem: The ratio of men to women in a plant is 7:5, and there are 24 more men than women. The total number of employees is:
q.why: Two parts equal 24, so one part is 12 and twelve parts is 144.

q.stem: A car covers 150 km in 2.5 hours. At the same speed, how long does 210 km take?
o: 3 hours
3.25 hours
3.5 hours
4 hours
q.why: Speed is 60 km/h. 210 ÷ 60 = 3.5.

q.stem: Pipe A fills a tank in 10 hours and pipe B in 15 hours. Together they fill it in:
o: 5 hours
6 hours
12.5 hours
25 hours
q.why: 1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6 of the tank per hour.

q.stem: A can finish a job in 12 days. A and B together finish it in 8 days. B alone would take:
o: 4 days
16 days
20 days
24 days

q.stem: A train 300 m long travels at 72 km/h. How long does it take to pass a signal post?
o: 12 seconds
15 seconds
20 seconds
24 seconds

q.stem: A lorry travels 60 km at 20 km/h and returns over the same 60 km at 30 km/h. Its average speed for the round trip is:
o: 24 km/h
25 km/h
26 km/h
q.why: Total time is 3 + 2 = 5 hours for 120 km.

q.why: The solutions are 4 and −1.

How many integers satisfy x² − 9 < 0?
q.why: −3 < x < 3: the integers −2 to 2.

q.why: x = 3 or x = −7.

What is the remainder when 2¹⁰ is divided by 7?
If n is an even integer, which of the following must be odd?
o: n²
q.why: 3n is even, so 3n + 1 is odd.

q.stem: The greatest common divisor of 84 and 126 is:
q.why: 84 = 2² × 3 × 7 and 126 = 2 × 3² × 7. The common part is 2 × 3 × 7.

q.stem: Three consecutive odd integers sum to 57. The smallest is:
q.why: The middle one is 19.

q.stem: The mean of 4, 8, 10, 14 and x is 10. What is x?
q.why: The sum must be 50, and the four known values add to 36.

q.stem: The median of 12, 7, 3, 9, 15 and 6 is:
q.why: Sorted: 3, 6, 7, 9, 12, 15. The median is the mean of 7 and 9.

q.stem: Ten numbers average 50. One of them, 95, is removed. The average of the remaining nine is:
Set A is {2, 4, 6} and set B is {12, 14, 16}. Which statement is true?
o: B has the larger standard deviation
A has the larger standard deviation
They have the same standard deviation
It cannot be determined
q.why: B is A with 10 added to each value, which leaves the spread unchanged.

q.stem: An outfit consists of one of 3 shirts, one of 4 pairs of trousers and one of 2 pairs of shoes. How many different outfits are possible?
In how many ways can 2 inspectors be chosen from a team of 7?
How many different arrangements are there of the letters in PLANT?
q.why: Five different letters: 5! = 120.

q.stem: A bin holds 5 red and 3 blue tokens. Two are drawn without replacement. The probability that both are red is:
An integer is chosen at random from 1 to 30. The probability that it is a multiple of 3 or of 5 is:
q.why: 10 multiples of 3, 6 of 5, and 2 of both: 14 out of 30.

A café chain introduced a loyalty app. Customers who use the app spend 12% more per visit than those who do not. The chain concludes that the app increases spending. Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
o: The app was expensive to develop.
Customers who installed the app were already the chain's highest spenders before it launched.
Some customers find the app hard to use.
Competing chains have similar apps.
q.why: If app users already spent more, the difference existed before the app and cannot be credited to it.

q.stem: A town replaced its streetlights with brighter lamps, and reported night-time burglaries fell 18% the following year. The council concludes that the new lights reduced burglary. Which of the following, if true, most weakens the conclusion?
o: The new lamps use less electricity.
Residents say they feel safer.
Burglaries fell by a similar amount in neighbouring towns that did not change their lights.
The lamps were installed on schedule.
q.why: A similar fall elsewhere points to a general cause, not the lights.

q.stem: A manufacturer plans to cut costs by buying a component from an overseas supplier whose unit price is 20% lower than the current supplier's. Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the plan?
o: The overseas supplier is a large company.
Freight, duty and the extra stock needed would add about 22% to the overseas unit cost.
The current supplier has been used for ten years.
The component is used in several products.
q.why: Total cost would be higher than now, so the plan would not cut costs.

q.stem: A company found that teams holding a daily stand-up meeting deliver projects faster than teams that do not. It will now require the meeting for all teams, expecting faster delivery everywhere. Which of the following, if true, most weakens this expectation?
o: The meetings last fifteen minutes.
Teams that adopted the meeting voluntarily were mostly working on smaller, simpler projects.
Some managers dislike meetings.
The company has forty teams.
q.why: Faster delivery may reflect simpler projects, not the meeting.

q.stem: A hospital introduced a surgical checklist, and its infection rate fell over the next year. The hospital argues that the checklist caused the fall. Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
o: The checklist has nineteen items.
Surgeons were trained in the checklist.
Infection rates at comparable hospitals without the checklist did not change over the same period.
The hospital also performs outpatient procedures.
q.why: A stable rate elsewhere rules out a general trend as the explanation.

q.stem: A retailer predicts that offering free delivery will raise its profit, because the number of orders will increase. Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the prediction?
o: Customers like free delivery.
The retailer's website was recently redesigned.
The average margin on an order is several times the cost of delivering it.
Delivery vans are leased, not owned.
q.why: The prediction is about profit. It holds only if extra orders earn more than delivery costs.

q.stem: An analyst predicts that a phone maker will gain market share because its new model has a longer battery life than rival models. Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the prediction?
o: The phone is available in four colours.
Surveys show battery life is the feature buyers in this segment weigh most heavily.
The maker has a large advertising budget.
Rival models were launched last year.
q.why: It links the stated advantage to what drives purchases.

q.stem: A city expects that adding protected bicycle lanes will reduce commuting by car. Which of the following, if true, most supports this expectation?
o: Bicycle sales rose last year.
The lanes will be painted green.
Many car commuters living within five kilometres of work say that the lack of safe lanes is their main reason for not cycling.
The city has a mild climate.
q.why: It shows that lanes address the reason current drivers do not cycle.

q.stem: Sales of a magazine fell after its cover price was raised. The publisher concludes that the price rise caused the fall. The argument assumes that:
o: The magazine is published monthly.
No other change, such as a general decline in magazine reading, accounts for the fall.
The price rise was large.
Advertising revenue also fell.
q.why: If something else explains the fall, the conclusion fails.

q.stem: A new machine produces 30% more units per hour than the one it replaces. The plant manager concludes that installing it will raise the plant's daily output by 30%. The argument assumes that:
o: The new machine is more reliable.
Operators will need training.
The stages before and after the machine can supply and absorb 30% more units.
The machine was bought at a discount.
q.why: If another stage limits the plant, a faster machine does not raise plant output.

q.stem: Customer complaints about a product fell by half this year. The firm concludes that product quality has improved. The argument assumes that:
o: Customers have not simply become less likely to complain, for example because complaining became harder.
The product is sold online.
Competitors also received fewer complaints.
The firm's sales rose.
q.why: Fewer complaints must reflect fewer problems for the conclusion to follow.

q.stem: Graduates of a training programme earn more than people who did not attend it. The organisers conclude that the programme raises earnings. The argument assumes that:
o: The programme is free.
Those admitted to the programme would not have earned more than the others in any case.
Graduates enjoyed the programme.
The programme lasts six months.
q.why: If participants were already abler or better connected, the gap is not due to the programme.

q.stem: All engineers in the design team know CAD. Some engineers in the design team also know simulation. No interns know simulation. Which of the following must be true?
o: Some interns know CAD.
All people who know simulation are in the design team.
Some people who know CAD are not interns.
No interns are in the design team.
q.why: The design engineers who know simulation know CAD and cannot be interns.

q.stem: A firm's revenue grew in each of the last five years. Its profit fell in two of those years. Which of the following must be true?
o: The firm cut prices in two years.
In at least two years, the firm's costs rose by more than its revenue did.
The firm's costs rose every year.
The firm made a loss in two years.
q.why: Profit is revenue minus cost. If revenue rose and profit fell, cost rose by more.

q.stem: Only suppliers holding certificate Q may submit a bid. Supplier Z submitted a valid bid. Which of the following must be true?
o: Supplier Z will win the contract.
All suppliers with certificate Q submitted bids.
Supplier Z holds certificate Q.
Supplier Z is the lowest bidder.
q.why: A valid bid requires the certificate.

q.stem: Furnaces account for most of a plant's energy use. This year the furnaces used 10% less energy, yet the plant's total energy use rose. Which of the following must be true?
o: The plant produced more units.
Energy use outside the furnaces rose by more than furnace energy use fell.
The furnaces were replaced.
Energy prices rose.
q.why: For the total to rise while one part falls, the rest must rise by more than that fall.

q.stem: A company plans to replace telephone support with a chatbot in order to cut costs without reducing customer satisfaction. Which of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the plan?
o: How many telephone agents the company employs.
What share of current telephone queries the chatbot can resolve without a human.
Which firm built the chatbot.
Whether competitors use chatbots.
q.why: If most queries still need a person, costs will not fall and satisfaction may.

q.stem: A farmer plans to switch to a drought-resistant seed that yields 10% less than ordinary seed in normal years, in order to raise average income over time. Which would be most useful to know?
o: How often droughts occur and how much ordinary seed loses in drought years.
The colour of the grain.
How many farmers use the new seed.
The size of the farm.
q.why: The trade is a small loss in normal years against a gain in drought years. Its value depends on how often and how large.

q.stem: A gym reports that members who use its personal trainers lose more weight than members who do not, and concludes that its trainers are effective. Which would be most useful to know in assessing this?
o: How much trainers are paid.
Whether members who choose trainers also attend more often and were more motivated to begin with.
What time the gym opens.
Whether the gym has a pool.
q.why: Motivation and attendance could explain the difference without the trainers.

q.stem: A bookshop cut the price of bestsellers by 30%, selling them at a loss, yet its total profit rose. Which of the following best explains this?
o: Bestsellers are heavily advertised.
Customers who came in for the cheap bestsellers also bought other books at full price.
The shop reduced its opening hours.
Publishers raised wholesale prices.
q.why: Profit on other books more than covered the loss on bestsellers.

q.stem: After the speed limit on a busy motorway was lowered, average journey times on it fell. Which of the following best explains this?
o: Drivers dislike lower limits.
Fuel consumption is lower at lower speeds.
At the lower limit there were fewer accidents and less stop-start congestion.
The motorway was built twenty years ago.
q.why: Steadier flow and fewer blockages can shorten journeys even at a lower top speed.

q.stem: A firm doubled its advertising spending this year, and its sales fell. Which of the following best explains this?
o: Advertising rates rose.
The firm's advertisements won an award.
A competitor launched a much cheaper equivalent product at the same time.
The firm hired a new agency.
q.why: A strong rival offer could outweigh the effect of the advertising.

q.stem: "Every successful start-up I studied had a founder who worked very long hours. So working long hours makes start-ups succeed." The reasoning is flawed because it:
o: Relies on the opinion of founders.
Fails to consider that founders of failed start-ups may have worked equally long hours.
Assumes that all start-ups succeed.
Defines success too narrowly.
q.why: Only survivors were studied. A trait common to them may be just as common among failures.

q.stem: "The committee's cost estimate must be wrong, because its chair once worked for the contractor." The reasoning is flawed because it:
o: Uses a sample that is too small.
Confuses cause and effect.
Attacks the source of the estimate instead of the evidence for it.
Assumes costs never change.
q.why: A possible bias is a reason to check the estimate, not proof that it is wrong.

q.stem: "If the line is balanced, output is stable. Output is stable. Therefore the line is balanced." The reasoning is flawed because it:
o: Treats a condition that is enough to produce a result as the only way to produce it.
Uses a term in two senses.
Relies on an unrepresentative sample.
Attacks an opponent.
q.why: Output could be stable for other reasons.

q.stem: "Sales rose in the three regions we surveyed, so sales rose across the whole country." The reasoning is flawed because it:
o: Confuses sales with profit.
Assumes prices were constant.
Generalises from a sample that may not represent the whole.
Relies on outdated figures.
q.why: Three regions may differ from the rest.

q.stem: The main point of the passage is that:
o: Trees do not cool cities.
Reflective roofs should replace tree planting.
The cooling a city gets from trees depends on water, species and time, so counting trees planted is a poor measure of success.
Dry cities should not plant trees.
q.why: The second paragraph states the conclusion drawn from the qualifications in the first.

q.stem: According to the passage, unirrigated trees in dry cities cool the air less during heat waves because they:
o: Lose their leaves.
Close their pores, which reduces evaporation.
Have narrow canopies.
Absorb heat like asphalt.
q.why: Stated directly in the first paragraph.

q.stem: The author would most likely agree that a city's tree programme should be judged mainly by:
o: The number of trees planted each year.
The money spent on planting.
The measured reduction in temperature it achieves.
The height of the trees.
q.why: The author contrasts measuring effort with measuring cooling.

q.stem: The sentence "None of this argues against planting" serves to:
o: Introduce a new objection to trees.
Prevent the reader from concluding that tree planting is not worthwhile.
Summarise the measurements of shaded streets.
Contradict the first paragraph.
q.why: It limits how far the preceding qualifications should be taken.

q.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to:
o: Argue that manufacturers should stop offering variety.
Describe an approach to the trade-off between variety and cost, and its limits.
Explain how trucks are designed.
Show that overhead costs are unimportant.
q.why: The first paragraph presents modular design. The second gives its costs and where it works best.

q.stem: According to the passage, the costs of product variety are easy to overlook because they:
o: Are very small.
Are paid by customers.
Accumulate in overhead and not in any one product's bill.
Occur only in the first year.
q.why: Stated in the first paragraph.

q.stem: It can be inferred that a module shared by a basic product and a premium product will most likely:
o: Be cheaper than a dedicated module for the premium product.
Exceed what the basic product requires.
Make both products identical.
Be redesigned every year.
q.why: A shared module must meet the most demanding requirement, so the less demanding product is over-served.

q.stem: The final sentence suggests that firms gain most from modular design when they:
o: Standardise everything the customer sees.
Offer as many variants as possible.
Allow variety where customers notice it and standardise elsewhere.
Avoid fixing interfaces.
q.why: That is the deliberate choice the sentence describes.

q.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Targets always corrupt organisations.
The four-hour target had no effect on patients.
A target can cause gaming and real improvement together, so it should be judged by its overall effect on the purpose.
Ambulances should not be used as waiting rooms.
q.why: The second paragraph qualifies the critics' view and states the authors' test.

q.stem: According to the passage, some hospitals held patients in ambulances because:
o: Emergency departments were closed.
The four-hour clock started only when a patient entered the department.
Ambulance crews requested it.
Patients preferred to wait outside.
q.why: Stated in the first paragraph.

q.stem: The fall in deaths within thirty days is mentioned in order to:
o: Show that the critics' evidence was fabricated.
Provide evidence that the target brought real improvement as well as gaming.
Argue that targets should be abolished.
Explain why patients were held in ambulances.
q.why: It supports the 'more qualified conclusion'.

q.stem: The study's authors would most likely assess a new performance target by asking:
o: Whether it changes anyone's behaviour.
Whether staff approve of it.
Whether the behaviour it rewards serves the underlying purpose better than before.
Whether it is easy to measure.
q.why: This restates their 'appropriate question'.

q.stem:
What is the value of x?
(1) 3x − 2 = 10
(2) x² = 16
o: Statement (1) alone is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not.
Statement (2) alone is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is.
Each statement alone is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) together are not sufficient.
q.why: Statement (1) gives x = 4. Statement (2) allows 4 or −4.

q.stem:
Is n greater than 0?
(1) n² > 0
(2) n³ > 0
o: Statement (1) alone is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not.
Statement (2) alone is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is.
Each statement alone is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) together are not sufficient.
q.why: A positive cube means a positive number. A positive square allows either sign.

q.stem:
What is the average of x and y?
(1) x + y = 18
(2) x − y = 4
o: Statement (1) alone is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not.
Statement (2) alone is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is.
Each statement alone is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) together are not sufficient.
q.why: The average is (x + y) ÷ 2 = 9. Statement (2) does not fix the sum.

q.stem:
Is the integer k divisible by 12?
(1) k is divisible by 4.
(2) k is divisible by 6.
o: Statement (1) alone is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not.
Statement (2) alone is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is.
Each statement alone is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) together are not sufficient.
q.why: Divisible by both 4 and 6 means divisible by their least common multiple, 12. Alone, 4 and 6 are counterexamples.

q.stem:
Is the integer k divisible by 8?
(1) k is divisible by 4.
(2) k is divisible by 6.
o: Statement (1) alone is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not.
Statement (2) alone is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is.
Each statement alone is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) together are not sufficient.
q.why: Both hold for 12, which is not divisible by 8, and for 24, which is.

q.stem:
What percentage of a firm's employees are engineers?
(1) The firm has 120 engineers.
(2) The firm has 280 employees who are not engineers.
o: Statement (1) alone is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not.
Statement (2) alone is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is.
Each statement alone is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) together are not sufficient.
q.why: Together the total is 400, so 30% are engineers.

q.stem:
Was the firm's profit higher this year than last year?
(1) Its revenue rose 8%.
(2) Its costs fell 3%.
o: Statement (1) alone is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not.
Statement (2) alone is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is.
Each statement alone is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) together are not sufficient.
q.why: Higher revenue and lower costs together guarantee higher profit. Either alone leaves the other free to offset it.

q.stem:
What is the price of one pen?
(1) 3 pens and 2 pencils cost ₹46.
(2) 6 pens and 4 pencils cost ₹92.
o: Statement (1) alone is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not.
Statement (2) alone is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is.
Each statement alone is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) together are not sufficient.
q.why: The second statement is the first doubled, so there is still one equation with two unknowns.

q.stem:
Is x greater than y?
(1) x ÷ y > 1
(2) y > 0
o: Statement (1) alone is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not.
Statement (2) alone is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is.
Each statement alone is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) together are not sufficient.
q.why: With y positive, x ÷ y > 1 gives x > y. Without it, x = −2 and y = −1 satisfy statement (1) with x smaller.

q.stem:
How many units did a plant make on Tuesday?
(1) It made 20% more units on Tuesday than on Monday.
(2) It made 2,200 units on Monday and Tuesday together.
o: Statement (1) alone is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not.
Statement (2) alone is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is.
Each statement alone is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) together are not sufficient.
q.why: Monday M and Tuesday 1.2M sum to 2,200, so M = 1,000 and Tuesday = 1,200.

q.stem:
Is the median of five numbers greater than their mean?
(1) Four of the numbers are each 10.
(2) The fifth number is less than 10.
o: Statement (1) alone is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not.
Statement (2) alone is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not.
Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is.
Each statement alone is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) together are not sufficient.
q.why: The median is 10. With the fifth below 10 the mean is below 10. Statement (1) alone allows the fifth to be 10 or higher.

q.stem:
Is the integer a odd?
(1) a + 3 is even.
(2) 2a is even.
o: Statement (1) alone is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not.
Statement (2) alone is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not.
